column1: # Unification is the most fundamental thing core does after dispatch, and
# until this file existed no corpus row touched it. The reason was
# structural rather than an oversight: unify's clients — `is`, `case`,
# typed defs, record shapes — are all basic/lang-layer words, so a bare
# core registry called the unifier from nowhere, and core/spec's notation
# could name seven builtin type literals and no type CONSTRUCTOR at all.
# Two additions open it, and both are in the established idiom:
#   unifyq a b   the fixture word, over core's own UnifyR / unifiesValue.
#                The PREDICATE half only — did the two values unify — not
#                the unified value: Go's UnifyR returns a meet and core/ts
#                has a predicate, so asking for the value would pin a port
#   d( … )       a disjunct of the listed items
#   [: T … ]     a typed list — child constraint, then retained elements
#   {: T k: v … }  a typed map, likewise
# The type-constructor forms are what make this corpus reach the surface
# the two ports actually differ on. Without them every candidate agreed:
# 70 of 70 over scalars, lattice roots, plain lists and plain maps. That
# negative result is worth as much as the divergences — it says the value
# subset core/ts implements is FAITHFUL, and the gap is entirely in the
# constructors it has no arm for.
# --- the shared subset: scalars, roots, plain containers -------------------
# Every one of these agreed on first measurement.
run unifyq { a: 1 b: 2 } { b: 2 a: 1 }
run unifyq { a: { b: 1 } } { a: { b: 1 } }
run unifyq { a: { b: 1 } } { a: { b: 2 } }
# --- type constructors: what the two ports DO agree on ---------------------
# The rest of this surface is in divergent.tsv; these are the rows that hold.
run unifyq true d( Integer String )
run unifyq d( Integer String ) Any
# Closed by the payload gate in unifiesValue: a typed map is no longer
# handed to asMap(), so these answer cleanly instead of throwing.
# --- a ROOT type literal is not `Any` to a disjunct ------------------------
# `Any` keeps a disjunct whole; nothing else does. core/go asked "is the
# value's Parent() Any", which is a CARRIER's question: a bare literal's
# Parent() is its LATTICE parent, and Scalar, Node, Ideal, Word and Type
# all sit directly under Any — so each of them passed for Any, and
# `d( 'a' )` unified with `Node`, an empty disjunct with `Scalar`. Found
# by the Lean model's differential search (spec/tools/diff-fuzz.py); the
# pairs below are the point — the same disjunct against `Any` still holds.
# The meet of two disjuncts is the disjunct of the pairwise meets of their
# alternatives; no pair unifying is no meet. (The kernel used to answer the
# FIRST alternative that matched — `Integer` for `Integer tor String`
# against itself — NUR386.) The rows below are the pairs with no meet, which
# both ports already refuse; the pairs that DO meet are in divergent.tsv,
# because core/ts's unifier has no disjunct arm at all.
# The EMPTY disjunct denotes the empty set, so it is `Never`: it meets
# `Never` and another empty disjunct, and nothing else.
run unifyq d( Integer String ) d( true none )
# Two map alternatives are two open patterns: a key both name must unify.
run unifyq d( { a: 1 } ) d( { a: 2 } )
# Reordered alternatives are one disjunct, as a typed container's child too.
run unifyq [: d( Integer String ) ] [: d( String Integer ) ]
# The same rule with a set of one on the other side: a type against a
# disjunct meets EVERY alternative (`Integer` against `5 tor 6` is
# `5 tor 6`, where the kernel answered `5`), and a type no alternative
# meets has no meet. A list or a map HOLDING a type is a shape, not a
# value, and is treated the same way; a map alternative stays an open
# pattern against it — the shape must carry the keys the pattern names.
run unifyq d( Integer String ) [: Integer ]
run unifyq d( { a: 1 } ) { b: Integer }
run unifyq d( { a: 1 } ) { a: String }
